Tattler
TAT-ler
noun
From the Middle Dutch and Middle English tatelen, “to prate, to chatter,” of imitative origin; hence an idle talker, a prater, one who tells what should not be told — a gossip and busybody.

Biblical Definition

A tattler is an idle prater — one whose tongue runs where it should be still, carrying tales from house to house and telling what ought never to be told. Paul names the sin in the younger widows who, left without useful labour, “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” (1Ti 5:13). Note the pedigree of the sin: idleness first, then wandering, then the busy tongue — the empty hour breeds the meddling word. Solomon warns against keeping such company: “He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips” (Pro 20:19). The tattler cannot hold a confidence; what he hears, he spends. And the tale, once loosed, is fuel: “Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth” (Pro 26:20). Take away the tattler and the quarrel dies for want of feeding. Behind all these stands the law of the LORD, which forbids the wandering tongue outright: “Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:16). The tattler thinks his words small coin, but “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Pro 18:21). What he scatters idly, God will weigh.

Webster 1828 Definition

An idle talker; a prater; one who tells tales and secrets that should not be told — a gossip.

TATTLER, one who prates; a telltale; an idle talker; one who reveals secrets.

From tatelen, “to prate, to chatter,” of imitative origin.

Its pedigree is idleness, then wandering, then the meddling tongue.

Paul names the tattling, busybody widows (1Ti 5:13).

The law forbids going up and down as a talebearer (Lev 19:16).

Key Scripture

1Ti 5:13 — "And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not."

Pro 20:19 — "He that goeth about as a talebearer revealeth secrets: therefore meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips."

Pro 26:20 — "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth."

Lev 19:16 — "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD."

Modern Corruption

An old word for the busy, meddling tongue; and the tattler now has instruments the ancient world never dreamed of, and calls his prating news.

expand to see more

The live sin is the tattler armed with a glowing screen. What Paul described — the idle who wander from house to house, speaking things they ought not — now travels at the speed of light and never leaves the chair. The feed of another’s troubles, the group chat that dissects a neighbour, the “prayer request” that is a confidence broken, the whole culture of oversharing that treats a private matter as public entertainment: these are the wandering tongue given wings. The age even flatters it, calling gossip “news” and idle meddling “keeping informed.” But Scripture strips the disguise. It roots the sin in idleness, warns that the talebearer reveals secrets, and forbids the saint to go up and down as one, for the tongue that will not keep a confidence will not keep a covenant either.

The grace that mortifies the tattler is the disciplined tongue that starves a quarrel and keeps a trust. Solomon gives the picture: where no wood is, the fire goes out, and where there is no talebearer, the strife ceases. Half the church’s conflicts would die overnight if no one carried the fuel. The Christian is called to be the man who withholds the wood — who covers a matter in love, who lets a confidence die with him, whose diligent hands leave no idle hour for the busy tongue to fill. And behind the whole duty stands the awful weight the tattler forgets: death and life are in the power of the tongue, and the God who signs His law “I am the LORD” will weigh every idle word. The remedy for a light tongue is a heavy sense of that reckoning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means an idle prater, a gossip, one who tells what ought not to be told.
